visuals.title: Quiz
visuals.text: Five questions. Answer along on the cards below the transcript, then hear Marco's answers.

quiz.pause_at: Pause here if you want to think it through

questions.q: A buyer finds cost savings of 100 a year before tax. Tax is 25%, the discount rate 10%, no growth. What are the savings worth?
questions.explain: 100 × (1 − 25%) = 75 after tax, and 75 ÷ 10% = 750. Capitalising the pre-tax 100 gives 1,000, the trap Sofia fell into.
questions.explain_at: Seventy-five over ten percent: seven hundred and fifty

questions.q: A target is worth 1,000 on its own and the net synergies are worth 600. What's the walk-away price?
questions.explain: Standalone value plus net synergies: 1,000 + 600. Paying it hands every bit of synergy to the sellers, so it's the ceiling, not the offer.

questions.q: Why do bankers trust cost synergies more than revenue synergies?

options.text: They don't reduce the tax bill

questions.explain: The buyer can close an office or sign a supply contract itself; revenue synergies depend on customers and competitors.
questions.explain_at: A cost saving is in the buyer's own hands

questions.q: What was the largest source of AB InBev's promised $1.4bn a year of savings from SABMiller?
questions.explain: Corporate and overlapping regional head offices were about 35% of the total; breweries and distribution about a quarter.

questions.q: Fairfax commits up to $2.3bn for half of Boots' equity, in a deal worth $8.9bn including debt. Roughly how much is debt?
questions.explain: $2.3bn is half the equity, so equity is up to about $4.6bn and debt about $8.9bn − $4.6bn = $4.3bn. Subtracting only Fairfax's cheque gives $6.6bn.
